title: Statutory interpretation and regulatory interpretation
summary: The identity of the text matters: Loper Bright addresses statutes enacted by Congress, while Kisor addresses an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations.
notes:
The statutory-review question concerns what legal authority Congress supplied. Loper Bright requires independent interpretation while respecting actual delegations and persuasive agency guidance. The regulatory-review question concerns the meaning of a rule made under that authority. Kisor retains conditional Auer deference when a regulation remains genuinely ambiguous and the agency’s reading satisfies the additional prerequisites. The source notes treat both as operative within the assigned account and emphasize that Roberts and Kavanaugh distinguished them in Kisor. (Printed 995–996, 1000–1001.)

There is a genuine theoretical tension. Kagan’s four-Justice discussion in Kisor reads § 706 as compatible with deferential interpretation and relies on pre-APA practice. Loper Bright’s majority reads the APA as requiring independent statutory judgment. The authors suggest possible explanations grounded in statutory language or historical practice, practical overlap between Kisor and persuasion, and the possibility of a future challenge. They present alternatives for analysis, not a later overruling. (Printed 1000–1001.)

The final problem asks whether a regulation could expressly entrust future interpretive rules with defining its ambiguous terms, drawing an analogy to an express statutory delegation recognized in Loper Bright. The question raises the agency’s authority to delegate interpretive control, § 553’s procedural distinction, § 706 review, and the separation-of-powers criticism of joining prescription with interpretation. The reading leaves the hypothetical unresolved. (Printed 1002.)
